s: bow, prow (of a ship), nose (of an aircraft)
Bug.et:
From Middle High German buoc (“animal shoulder”), from Old High German buog (“animal shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōgu, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz (“arm; shoulder”). More at English bough.
The common contemporary meaning “bow” (early 17th c.) is a sem…

s: synonym of Biegung (“curve, place or way of bending”)
Bug.et: From Middle High German buoc, deverbal from biegen.
From Polish Bug and Russian Буг (Bug).

s: a handle such as that of a bucket
Bügel.et: From Middle High German *bügel (attested as bügele f, later bogell m [15th c.]), from Proto-Germanic *bugilaz, from the root of *beuganą (“to bend, bow”). Cognate with Dutch beugel, Middle Low German bȫgel (earlier already Old Saxon armbugil), Old Norse bygill…

bügeln.et: Back-formation from Bügeleisen (literally “iron with a bow, bail, handle”). By surface analysis, Bügel + -en.

Bügeleisen.et: From Bügel (“bent piece of metal; bow, bail, handle”) + Eisen (“iron”). Now commonly reanalyzed as bügeln (“to iron”) + Eisen, but the verb is in fact a backformation.

s: to put something in a place; to move something
bugsieren.et: Borrowed from Dutch boegseren, from Portuguese puxar with influence of boeg (the cognate of German Bug (“bow of a ship”)), from Latin pulsare. Doublet of pulsieren.

Bugdoll.et: From Silesian or Polish Bugdoł, Bógdoł.

s: bow saw (a lightweight metal-framed saw in the shape of a bow with a removable coarse wide blade, used for cutting tree trunks)
hacksaw (fine-toothed, frame-mounted saw used to cut metal)

Bügelkrone.et: From Bügel (“ball, clamp, yoke”) + Krone (“crown; coronet”).
